title: A state-funded grocery-card bridge can cushion SNAP exit without proving durable food security
source_unit: Connecticut state-funded grocery assistance for residents losing SNAP eligibility
geography: Connecticut residents pushed out of SNAP by federal work-rule changes

denominator.unit: roughly Connecticut residents expected to lose SNAP eligibility under the announced plan; actual distributed-recipient count not disclosed

state_funding.unit: U.S. dollars from Connecticut's Federal Cuts Response Fund

delivery_channel.value: Prepaid virtual grocery cards distributed through community action agencies, not loaded onto existing EBT cards

eligibility_route.value: Individuals who lost SNAP eligibility because of the federal changes and received a DSS notice showing the three-month limit could request the benefit; eligibility was confirmed at request

persistence_rule.value: The card does not expire and unused balance remains until spent

reentry_support.value: Community action agencies distribute cards and connect recipients with supports intended to help regain SNAP eligibility

observations.method: Structured extraction from Connecticut's official funding and distribution announcements; expected population, benefit amount, funding, distribution, eligibility, use, and reentry-support stages are kept separate from actual receipt and food outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The public announcements do not disclose actual eligible, requested, approved, distributed, activated, or spent counts; card adequacy, food security, household substitution, SNAP reentry, trust, and exit remain unmeasured.
observations.subgroup: Connecticut individuals who lost SNAP eligibility under the stated federal work-rule changes; the expected 25,000 population is not an observed recipient denominator.
observations.counterinterpretation: A one-time $300 virtual grocery card can cushion an abrupt benefit exit and preserve reentry support while still leaving duration, adequacy, access, and durable household security uncertain.

related_sources.claim: The June plan announced roughly 25,000 expected residents, $8.5 million in funding, and $300 grocery cards for people losing SNAP eligibility.
Connecticut DSS describes the community-action-agency distribution route for the one-time $300 grocery card.
The maintained Connecticut SNAP Eligibility 2026 page repeats the August 4 community-action-agency referral for the $300 grocery card but publishes no distribution, spending, or reentry totals.

boundary: This record establishes a state-funded bridge from SNAP eligibility loss to a defined grocery-card distribution route and reentry-support intention. It does not establish individual eligibility confirmation, card receipt, spending, food adequacy, SNAP reentry, trust, or durable household recovery.
